summary: In Jericho, Jesus calls a rich chief tax collector down from a sycamore tree, stays at his house, and declares that salvation has come to it.
key_insight: Luke says Zacchaeus “sought to see who Jesus was.” Jesus ends by saying He came “to seek and to save that which was lost.” Luke uses the same word for seeking. Zacchaeus climbed a tree to look for Jesus, but Jesus had come looking for him.
story: Jesus had just given a blind beggar his sight near Jericho. Now He entered the city and was passing through. A man named Zacchaeus lived there, a chief tax collector, and he was rich.

Zacchaeus wanted to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, for he was a short man. So he ran ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was going to pass that way.
When Jesus came to the place, He looked up and saw him. “Zacchaeus, make haste and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” Zacchaeus hurried down and received Him joyfully.
Everyone who saw it began to complain, saying, “He has gone to be a guest with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold.”
Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham; for the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost.”

scene.label: A chief tax collector
scene.text: This is the only place in the New Testament where the title appears. Jericho sat on the trade road from across the Jordan and was famous for its palms and balsam, so customs duties there were rich. Zacchaeus probably oversaw other collectors and profited from their work.

scene.label: The sycamore
scene.text: The sycamore-fig grows in the warm Jordan valley. It has a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb. The prophet Amos tended its fruit (Amos 7:14). It is a different tree from the sycamore of North America.

scene.label: Running and climbing
scene.text: A wealthy man of position would not normally run in the street or climb a tree in public. Zacchaeus set his dignity aside to see Jesus.

scene.label: Fourfold
scene.text: The Law made a thief who had killed or sold a stolen sheep repay four sheep (Exodus 22:1). For goods taken by fraud and confessed, it required the full amount plus a fifth (Numbers 5:7). Zacchaeus held himself to the penalty for theft, far more than the Law asked of a man who confessed, and gave away half his wealth besides.

scene.label: His name
scene.text: Zacchaeus is the Greek form of a Hebrew name related to a word for pure or righteous (compare Zaccai in Ezra 2:9). He was a Jew, and Jesus calls him “a son of Abraham.”

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells of Zacchaeus. He places him a few verses after the rich ruler who went away sorrowful (18:18–27), so here is a rich man who does enter, giving without being told, a living answer to the disciples’ question, “Who then can be saved?” Jesus’ closing words sum up Luke’s whole Gospel (19:10).

seeing.reveals: Jesus calls Zacchaeus by name and says, “today I must stay at your house.” He does not wait to be invited, and He does not wait for Zacchaeus to change first. He is the Son of Man who seeks the lost.
seeing.living: Zacchaeus changed after Jesus welcomed him, not before, and the change reached his money at once. Receive Jesus as he did, quickly and joyfully, and let His grace reach the place where you have taken more than your share.
seeing.ponder: What would it look like for salvation to come to your house today, all the way down to what you own?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus came looking for Zacchaeus, and grace turned a grasping man into a generous one.
outline: A Savior who calls by name (5–6)
preaching.watch_for: Read 18:43 with 19:7. When Jesus healed the blind beggar, “all the people” gave praise to God; when He went home with the tax collector, “they all complained.” Luke’s word “today” (19:5, 9) rings through his Gospel (4:21; 23:43).
